## Summary
The company’s capital expenditures were only 68% of its depreciation, meaning it spent less on replacing or adding long-term assets than the estimated amount those assets lost in value during the period. If this pattern continues, it may indicate underinvestment, an aging asset base, or potential pressure on future operating capacity; however, capital spending can vary significantly from year to year, so the trend should be reviewed over several periods. This figure alone does not indicate whether the company is overvalued or undervalued, as that requires information such as earnings, cash flow, debt, and market price. Future performance could weaken if underinvestment reduces productivity or growth, although lower spending may be reasonable if management is deliberately operating with fewer capital needs.

Apple delivered strong momentum, with total sales up 16% year over year, led by iPhone—especially Pro models—Services, Mac, Europe, Greater China and the Americas; new operating systems and Siri AI could support future demand, while $14.9 billion of deferred revenue provides some visibility. However, valuation and future profits face meaningful risks: rising semiconductor, memory, cloud-computing and AI-infrastructure costs may pressure margins, while tariffs, currency movements, product-launch timing and seasonal demand could increase volatility or reduce sales. Apple also has substantial financial commitments, including $82.3 billion of fixed-rate notes, $27.6 billion of remaining employee stock-compensation costs, nearly $28 billion of unconditional purchase obligations, and large ongoing buybacks and dividends, although cash generation and debt-market access currently appear sufficient. Customer and vendor receivables are increasingly concentrated, and long-duration securities, debt hedges and foreign-currency exposures remain sensitive to interest rates and exchange rates. The most significant strategic risks are escalating antitrust and App Store litigation, EU Digital Markets Act requirements, privacy regulation and potential restrictions on Google search payments, which could force business-model changes, reduce high-margin Services commissions, trigger substantial fines, or materially affect revenue, profitability and the share price.
